headlines.summary: Automakers including Ford, Rivian and GM are expanding 3D printing to make prototypes, factory tools and low-volume parts faster and at lower cost.
headlines.article_text: How Rivian, Ford and GM are using 3D printing to reduce costs Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Automakers such as Ford, Rivian and GM are expanding 3D printing beyond prototyping into making factory tools and selected production parts. Automakers say additive manufacturing can shorten development and repair cycles and reduce costs for low-volume needs. Rivian says it has invested more than $5 million in 3D-printing machines and is widening employee access to the technology. In this article RIVN F GM SSYS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:27 02:27 The rise of 3D-printed car parts Digital Original DETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing. Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs. "At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jared Beck, head of Rivian's additive manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company." The benefits of 3D printing Also known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals. The progression of the new steering wheel for Rivian's new R2 SUV from 3D print to finished design for production at its facility in Plymouth, Michigan. Michael Wayland / CNBC Printers can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins. Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually. Beck said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours. "It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Beck said. The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand. A 3D-printed version of Rivian's cartoon Yeti mascot named Gary stands inside an additive manufacturing area at Rivian's facility in Plymouth, Michigan. Michael Wayland / CNBC "3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Beck said. Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds. GM, Ford There's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors , which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants. Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters. Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer, holds up a device he 3D printed to reinstall vehicle badges onto the automaker's F-150 pickup trucks inside the River Rouge factory in Dearborn, Michigan. Michael Wayland / CNBC "By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge." Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive. Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks. Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost. Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available. A table full of 3D-printed parts and tools inside the 3D-printing lab at Ford's River Rouge factory in Dearborn, Michigan. Michael Wayland / CNBC "They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said. Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said. GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification. The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob. Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing. "The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense." headlines.article_text: Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Days after Anthropic released its highly anticipated IPO prospectus, Microsoft, Google and Amazon released quarterly results that added to market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has already been concerned that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows, leading to fears that capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty Images Anthropic picked a tough week to unveil its IPO prospectus . Within days of its release, several of the company's key partners, including Microsoft , Google and Amazon , reported quarterly results that added fuel to existing market jitters around the artificial intelligence buildout. "Everybody's still full steam ahead on AI, but all the things around it took an interesting turn this week," Daniel Newman, CEO at Futurum Group, told CNBC in an interview on Friday. The hyperscalers' results have "raised eyebrows" and created a new headwind in the market, which is "more doubt on capital structure," he said. No matter the current state of the market, Anthropic was going to have to address a skeptical investor base as it pursues a potentially record-setting initial public offering in the coming weeks. In its prospectus on Monday, the AI company disclosed a net loss for the first half of the year of $80 billion, alongside hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors . Investors are still waiting to see Anthropic's third-quarter financials. Heading into this week, fears were mounting about the financial health of neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius , which are facing rising borrowing costs and a dearth of lenders as they pursue aggressive AI buildouts. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX , but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible. Now investors are growing increasingly worried about the whole AI trade. "It's a great technology, seems to do things that we never would have imagined, but how does that then translate into a viable business?" David Hsu, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania Wharton School, said in an interview. The Nasdaq Composite notched its first three-week losing streak since March after plunging 2.9% on Friday . Nvidia , whose graphics processing units have powered the AI boom, traded lower, along with the whole semiconductor sector, after Intel issued a weak forecast, sending its stock to its steepest drop since the 1970s. Microsoft, Google and Amazon all had notes of concern this week in their reports. The companies have been on a spending blitz in recent years to meet the surge in demand for AI infrastructure, but all three issued capex figures or forecasts that came in below analysts' estimates. Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, while Alphabet maintained its guidance for up to $205 billion and Amazon reiterated its roughly $220 billion forecast. "It's been an ugly reporting season for tech thus far," Jonathan Krinsky, managing director at BTIG, wrote in a Thursday note. He described the fallout as "The Techsas Chainsaw Massacre," adding that there's too much weakness in the sector for the market to ignore. Cash is becoming an issue. Amazon reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, recording an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing 12-month period. Google reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, one reason the stock tanked almost 13% on Thursday, its worst day ever. Microsoft maintained positive free cash flow of $18.6 billion, but it's down significantly for a second straight quarter. The company announced plans on Thursday to raise $25 billion in bonds , as it seeks additional sources of funding to help finance its infrastructure expansion. "Suddenly, they're like, 'We can't keep funding this on free cash flow,'" Newman said. "The worry is that basically now there's no company that's able to do this using their own business capabilities to create cash flow. It's becoming increasingly alarming." Cloud growth remains strong Anthropic's hyperscaler partners are also among its biggest investors. The companies all need each other to keep the flywheel turning, a topic that's sure to be a major point of discussion in Anthropic's upcoming roadshow. Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. A big tail wind for Anthropic remains AI demand. Microsoft, Google and Amazon all reported cloud growth that topped analysts' estimates, with revenue in Google's business more than doubling from a year earlier. And Oracle , one of the biggest spenders on AI data centers, said at its investor day on Wednesday that it will limit additional fundraising in the coming years to $20 billion, and will turn cash flow positive in the second half of next fiscal year. Analysts at Citizens wrote in a Thursday report that the announcement "put the biggest investor fear to rest — that funding its enormous AI infrastructure buildout would require an open-ended increase in debt and equity issuance." watch now VIDEO 4:11 04:11 Big Tech earnings put AI spending and profitability in focus: Analyst Access Middle East Attention will now turn back from hyperscaler earnings to Anthropic, as investors assess how much risk they're willing to assume and at what price. The IPO market has largely been frozen since SpaceX's record offering in June. Biometric ring maker Oura , Australian AI data center operator Firmus and SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm subsidiary have all recently postponed or abandoned plans to IPO . Nscale, a neocloud that filed to go public in September , hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks, nor has SoftBank's SB Energy .
